slides.title: Inheritance

blocks.text: Inheritance is an important and powerful feature for reusing software. Suppose you need to define classes to model circles, rectangles, and triangles. These classes have many common features. What is the best way to design these classes to avoid redundancy and make the system easy to comprehend and easy to maintain? The answer is to use inheritance.

In Java terminology, a class C that extends another class B is called a subclass, and B is called a superclass. A superclass is also referred to as a parent class or a base class, and a subclass as a child class, an extended class, or a derived class. A subclass inherits accessible data fields and methods from its superclass and may also add new data fields and methods.

slides.title: Using the keyword super

blocks.text: The keyword this references the calling object.
The keyword super refers to the superclass. It can be used to:
1. Call a superclass constructor 2. Call a superclass method
Unlike data fields and methods, the constructors of a superclass are not inherited by a subclass. They can only be invoked from the constructors of the subclasses using the keyword super, as follows:

super();
super(arguments);
If super is not used explicitly, the superclass's no-arg constructor is automatically invoked.

slides.title: Overriding Methods in the Superclass

blocks.text: A subclass inherits methods from a superclass. Sometimes it is necessary for the subclass to modify the implementation of a method defined in the superclass. This is referred to as method overriding.

slides.title: NOTE

blocks.text: An instance method can be overridden only if it is accessible.
A private method cannot be overridden, because it is not accessible outside its own class.
If a method defined in a subclass is private in its superclass, the two methods are completely unrelated.
Like an instance method, a static method can also be inherited. However, a static method cannot be overridden.
If a static method defined in the superclass is redefined in a subclass, the method defined in the superclass is hidden.

slides.title: The toString() method in Object

blocks.text: The toString() method returns a string representation of the object.
The default implementation returns a string consisting of a class name of which the object is an instance, the @ sign, and a number representing the object’s memory address in hexadecimal.

Loan loan = new Loan();
System.out.print(loan.toString());
The code displays something like Loan@15037e5 . This message is not very helpful or informative.
Usually, you should override the toString method so that it returns a readable string representation of the object.
You can pass an object to System.out.print(object). This is
equivalent to System.out.print(object.toString()).

slides.title: Polymorphism and Dynamic Binding

blocks.text: Method m takes a parameter of the Object type.
You can invoke it with any subtype of Object.
This feature is known as polymorphism.
When the method m(Object x) is executed,
the x.toString() method is invoked.
x may be an instance of GraduateStudent,
Object have their own implementation of the toString() method.
The used toString() method will be determined dynamically at runtime. This capability is known as dynamic binding.

slides.title: Dynamic Binding

blocks.text: Dynamic binding works as follows: Suppose an object o is an instance of classes C1, C2, ..., and Cn, where C1 is a subclass of C2, C2 is a subclass of C3, ..., and Cn-1 is a subclass of Cn.

In Java, Cn is the Object class. If o invokes a method p, the JVM searches the implementation for the method p in C1, C2, ..., Cn-1 and Cn, in this order, until it is found. Once an implementation is found, the search stops, and the first-found implementation is invoked.

slides.title: Method Matching versus Binding

blocks.text: Matching a method signature and binding a method implementation are two different issues.
The compiler finds a matching method according to parameter type, number of parameters, and order of the parameters at compilation time.
A method may be implemented in several subclasses. The
Java Virtual Machine dynamically binds the implementation of the method at runtime.

slides.title: Casting Objects

blocks.text: You have already used the casting operator to convert variables of one primitive type to another. Casting can also be used to convert an object of one class type to another within an inheritance hierarchy.
Object o = new Student(); // Implicit casting
The above statement is legal because an instance of Student is automatically an instance of Object (Student is a subclass of Object).
Suppose you want to assign the object reference o to a variable of the
Student type using the following statement:

Student b = o;
                              // Compiler error
The compiler generates an error because an Object o is not a subtype of
Student. To tell the compiler o is indeed a Student object, use explicit casting, as follows:

Student b = (Student) o;
                              // Explicit casting

slides.title: The instanceof Operator

blocks.text: It is always possible to cast an object of a subclass to an object of a superclass, known as upcasting or implicit casting.
When casting an object of a superclass to an object of its subclass, known as downcasting, explicit casting must be used using the cast notation.

For the casting to be successful, you must make sure the object to be casted is an instance of the subclass. If the superclass object is not an instance of the subclass, a runtime ClassCastException occurs.
Use the instanceof operator to test if an object is an instance of a class:

slides.title: Visibility or Accessibility Modifiers

blocks.text: The modifiers private, protected, and public are known as visibility or accessibility modifiers because they specify how classes and class members are accessed. The visibility of these modifiers increases in this order:
Visibility increases private, default (no modifier), protected, public
A protected data or method in a public class can be accessed by any class in the same package or its subclasses, even if the subclasses are in a different package.

slides.raw_text:
Visibility or Accessibility Modifiers
❑The modifiers private, protected, and public are 
known as visibility or accessibility modifiers because they 
specify how classes and class members are accessed. The 
visibility of these modifiers increases in this order:
Visibility increases
private, default (no modifier), protected, public
❑A protected data or method in a public class can be 
accessed by any class in the same package or its subclasses, 
even if the subclasses are in a different package.

slides.title: Data and Methods Visibility

blocks.text: Use the private modifier to hide the members of the class completely so they cannot be accessed directly from outside the class.
Use no modifier (the default) to allow members of the class to be accessed directly from any class within the same package but not from other packages.
Use the protected modifier to enable members of the class to be accessed by the subclasses in any package or classes in the same package.
Use the public modifier to enable members of the class to be accessed by any class.

slides.title: Notes

blocks.text: The private and protected modifiers can be used only for members of the class, but not for the class itself.
The public modifier and the default modifier (no modifier) can be used on members as well as on the class.
A class with no modifier cannot be accessed by classes from other packages. However, it can be accessed by classes in the same package.
A subclass may override a protected method in its superclass and change its visibility to public.
A subclass cannot weaken the accessibility of a method defined in the superclass. For example, if a method is defined as public in the superclass, it must be defined as public in the subclass.
